en: In that case, the value of what you received was retroactively reshaped, and your legitimate expectation was frustrated. This can be treated as misleading advertising by omission and as a breach of the offer. The response can include refunding what was paid, reducing the price or compensating with something that serves the same function, plus losses and damages if there is further harm. This is not mere discomfort on your part. It is a loss that Brazilian consumer law knows how to handle.

If, after a period, the same item reappears in an alternative store, in a special currency, in an aggressive promotion or at a significantly lower price, and if the temporal limitation of the exclusivity was not adequately and comprehensibly disclosed at the time of acquisition, there is a retroactive reconfiguration of the value delivered, with frustration of legitimate expectation and violation of transparency.<1>p. 214</1>
Scarcity, here, may operate as a device for capturing consent under informational inadequacy, with potential classification as misleading advertising by omission and breach of the offer<1>p. 214</1>

The legal consequence does not end with subjective discomfort, since the subsequent alteration of the attribute that justified the price may demand material restoration through the typical channels of consumer law, by restitution, price reduction or equivalent functional compensation, and may also open room for losses and damages when additional harm arising from the positional deception is demonstrated.<1>p. 214</1>

And what risk do you need to protect yourself from? Not the risk of the skin breaking, like a defective fridge. It is the risk of falling behind, of not belonging, of losing status, of seeing the skin you wanted go out of circulation and of seeing the image you built in there lose value.

This risk is not natural, because the platform calibrates it. It organizes time into seasons, goals and missions, rotates the catalog, creates progression systems that demand hours of repetition and applies automatic punishments. Missions show the mechanism clearly, because they work as a simple trade where you do something and get something, and they turn your time into currency without ever calling it work. Nobody forces you to buy, and yet the pressure is there, made of dependence and fear of missing out. Consumption becomes anxiety management.

In environments of continuous enjoyment, the most effective risk is not the risk of the product “not working”, which would correspond to a classic grammar of quality defect by inadequacy.<1>p. 211</1>

The decisive risk is the risk of loss of opportunity, the risk of falling behind, the risk of not belonging, the risk of losing status, the risk of seeing the desired object go out of circulation and the risk of the symbolic identity built in the ecosystem suffering depreciation. This risk is not natural.<1>p. 211</1>

It is calibrated by the platform through a temporal architecture, with seasons, splits, goals and missions. It is also calibrated by an architecture of supply, with rotation, scheduled exclusions and variable catalogs. Added to this are an architecture of reward, with progression systems and grind, and a sanctioning architecture, with bans, restrictions, automated penalties and opaque policies.<1>p. 211</1>
In terms of political economy, it is the typical gesture of turning time into currency without ever calling it work<1>p. 211</1>
Coercion appears neither as violence, nor as direct prohibition, nor as an explicit imposition to buy<1>p. 210</1>
Consumption, in this register, becomes anxiety management.<1>p. 210</1>
<1>Architectural teleology</1><2><3>Architectural teleology</3></2>

Teleology means purpose, what a thing is for. Here, the word says that none of this is a marketing accident. These are design choices that point in one direction, which is to extract more value from whoever is there, and not just to efficiently organize something that was naturally limited.

This purpose is not hidden in a secret document. It shows in the way the screen organizes what you see, what you calculate and the risk you feel. And it becomes important to the law when it stops being just commercial strategy and starts to hide or frustrate the correspondence between what was promised and what was delivered.

[...] the asymmetry is not limited to the supplier's “better knowledge”. It materializes in the supplier's very capacity to define what exists, for how long it exists, under what conditions it exists and under which narratives it exists [...] For this reason, artificial scarcity must be understood as part of an architectural teleology. It is part of a set of design choices oriented toward extraction and not toward the mere efficient organization of a naturally limited resource<1>p. 214</1>

It is part of a set of design choices oriented toward extraction and not toward the mere efficient organization of a naturally limited resource, and it is at this threshold that it ceases to be merely commercial strategy and becomes a legally relevant category for qualifying the deviation of purpose when the equivalence between promise and delivery is made opaque or deliberately frustrated<1>p. 214</1>
Architectural teleology manifests itself not only in clauses and policies, but in the way the interface organizes visibility, calculation and risk.<1>p. 214</1>
<1>Political economy</1>Invisible labor

And there is the work nobody calls work. You test new versions of the game before they come out, point out bugs, send suggestions, post, comment, make memes, write guides, record videos and stream. All of this gives the game visibility, explains the catalog to others and keeps desire alive.

For the company, this is worth a lot, because it lowers the cost of testing the game and works as advertising. But the contract treats your ideas as something the company can use freely, without paying anything. And whoever does this as a content creator looks like a small independent entrepreneur, when in practice they work as the public face of the business itself, under rules the company can change or withdraw. It is production that appears as participation.

Here the user is not only measured but mobilized as a distributed workforce that reduces quality control costs, widens the bug detection surface and feeds the supplier's organizational intelligence, producing a productivity that appears not as work, but as participation<1>p. 218</1>

In the Policy on unsolicited idea submissions, the supplier declares that it “values” feedback, but simultaneously structures the regime of appropriation, by reserving for itself the free use of ideas, suggestions and creative materials sent by the user, without this generating economic consideration, compensation or a duty of acknowledgment<1>p. 218</1>

generated by users themselves, such as posts, comments, streams, memes, guides and reviews, which becomes an engine of visibility and recommendation and works, in practice, as invisible labor of production and marketing of the IOC<1>p. 219</1>

Among the most conspicuous forms of this invisible labor is the work of content creators, streamers and influencers who orbit the ecosystem as if they were autonomous “microentrepreneurs”, when, in practice, they function as an intense public face of the incorporated exterior.<1>p. 219</1>
the very possibility of monetizing content depend on private, revocable and selective rules<1>p. 219</1>
<1>Political economy</1>Digital lumpenproletariat

Whoever produces value this way ends up in a strange place. They play a large part in production, but outside any category of work, employment or provision of services. They have no contract and no wage, and nobody recognizes them as someone who works.

At the same time, your progress, your status, your reputation and even your access depend on someone else's decisions, like those of a worker who lives under conditions set by the boss. The word lumpenproletariat names those who work on the margins, without the rights of those who work. Applied here, it describes someone who is a consumer and, at the same time, labor, without the law seeing that second part.

The consumer-user of platforms is formally outside the wage relation and outside the classic categories of work that sustained industrial dogmatics, but they are materially incorporated into the valorization regime as a constant source of diffuse productivity and as a base of support for the toll. From this point of view, the consumer approaches a digital lumpenproletariat: they participate intensely in the production of value, but do so on an opaque plane, outside the traditional categories of work, employment contract or provision of services.<1>p. 223</1>

When progress, status, reputation and the very continuity of access to the Immaterial Object of Consumption become dependent on unilateral decisions of the platform, the consumer finds themselves in a position analogous to that of the worker subjected to living conditions defined by others, but without the law recognizing them as such.<1>p. 223</1>
The “cloud serf” produces without a contract, without a wage and without recognition as work.<1>p. 223</1>

[...] but as manifestations of a common structural arrangement, marked by platform technofeudalism, digital rentierism and a specific form of exploitation of the consumer who, contextually, is also characterized as incorporated external workforce (the “consumer-worker”)<1>p. 143</1>
<1>Political economy</1>Intellectual property as a fence

Intellectual property is the set of rights that protects creations, such as the design of a skin, the music of a game and the code that makes everything work. It exists to encourage those who create. But, in an online game, it does more than protect the work. It helps the company define who can use what, for how long and under what conditions.

When these rights are combined with licenses, accounts, copy locks, catalogs and passwords, the incentive to create can become a fence. Circulating becomes infringement and enjoying becomes a matter of permission. That is why intellectual property does not appear here as an outside detail, but as a piece of the very structure that encloses the game and your collection inside it. And competition between companies changes, because it stops being about a better product and becomes about who fences in more and holds on better.

Once stabilized, the code tends to reproduce itself through institutional inertia, path dependencies and legal and economic mechanisms that make alternatives and reappropriations more expensive. In this scenario, intellectual property appears as an infrastructure of semiotic and technical governance. It not only protects creations, but contributes to delimiting uses, restricting reconfigurations and consolidating the supplier's authority over the conditions of enjoyment<1>p. 130</1>
When this decision is coupled with license agreements, accounts, DRM<1>p. 234</1>

catalogs and authentication mechanisms, the incentive to create gives way to a technology of blocking, so that circulation is treated as infringement and enjoyment is converted into authorization. In this context, competition ceases to be merely a dispute over products and becomes a dispute over enclosures.<1>p. 234</1>
It is here that intellectual property rights cease to appear as a peripheral legal title and begin to operate as a material component of the architecture of closure.<1>p. 234</1>

The competitive mutation described manifests itself clearly in platform-operated interactive entertainment because competitive value is not concentrated in the “quality” of an isolated good, but in the capacity to keep the consumer bound to a proprietary grammar of belonging, progress and distinction<1>p. 232</1>
<1>Identity captivity</1><2><3>Identity captivity</3></2>

So why not leave? Because leaving costs more than money. When you leave, you lose the recognition, the reputation and the history you built there, recorded in rankings, collections, histories and signs of distinction that only exist inside that game.

This dependence is not a weakness of yours or something in your head. It comes from the way the place is set up, because it is the platform that defines what counts as value, as belonging and as progress, and that can downgrade or erase all of it. Over time, the toll stops being the price of an item and becomes the fee for keeping your place. Giving this a name does not create a new good. Its purpose is to make this form of loss visible and controllable.

[...] reinforcing a circuit of permanence that converts the individual's participation into an input of valorization for the platform. This effect can be named, with operational precision, identity captivity, understood as a modality of dependence in which the cost of exit is not reduced to the patrimonial plane, but involves loss of recognition, of reputation and of narrative continuity objectified in public records of performance, collections, histories and signs of distinction produced within the ecosystem.<1>p. 224-225</1>

Dependence, in this register, is not psychological in the individualizing sense, but institutional and semiotic, because it derives from a regime of visibility and sanction that defines what counts as value, belonging and legitimate progress and, correlatively, defines how this can be downgraded, erased or discredited.<1>p. 225</1>
In consumer law terms, the relevance of the concept is not to create a new good, but to make a specific form of loss in the fact of consumption controllable<1>p. 225</1>
The result is identity captivity, in which the toll stabilizes as a fee for maintaining one's place, not as a one-off price for an item.<1>p. 258</1>
So is having a store, a currency and rare items illegal?

None of this makes it illegal to have a store, a currency of its own, events or rare items. Creating scarcity is commercial strategy, and strategy, on its own, is not unlawful. It starts to matter to the law when it hides or frustrates the correspondence between what was promised and what was delivered, as in the case of the exclusivity that had a time limit nobody mentioned.

For this reason, artificial scarcity must be understood as part of an architectural teleology. It is part of a set of design choices oriented toward extraction and not toward the mere efficient organization of a naturally limited resource, and it is at this threshold that it ceases to be merely commercial strategy and becomes a legally relevant category for qualifying the deviation of purpose when the equivalence between promise and delivery is made opaque or deliberately frustrated<1>p. 214</1>
<1>Owning the work is not an excuse for everything</1><2>Owning the work is not an excuse for everything</2>
When do the rights over the game become a shield?

When the company uses the rights it holds over the game to resist any control over the way it supplies what you bought. This includes copyright, trade secrets, licenses and control over the system itself.

It is worth understanding the role of these rights. Intellectual property does not appear here only as an obstacle coming from outside. It is what helps the company define what can be used, for how long and under what conditions. It protects creation, but it also establishes the company's authority over the way you use what you bought. That is why it is part of the very structure of what is sold.
How should the company use exclusivity?

By using exclusivity without turning it into a shield to hide everything, worsen what you bought or take away your access without reason. The balance between the company's rights and yours is struck through the social function, according to which these rights also exist to serve the interest of society. And it is struck through the limits the Brazilian Federal Constitution imposes on whoever exercises private power.
How do you assess the justification for the restriction?
Whether the restriction the company invokes is really necessary to protect the game and the work, or whether it is serving to shield the way it governs the environment.
What can you ask for when the company invokes the work?

That consumer law keeps applying. In practice, this may mean a delimited examination of the records that preserves the secrets, and control over the equivalence of what you bought. It may also mean that the company respects the duties of adequacy, transparency and restoration. And, if the game is shut down, that the exit comes, as far as possible, with transition, preservation or transfer of what you had in there.
Does the company lose its rights over the game?

The intellectual property rights over the game, the art and the code remain protected. Nobody asks the company to give up the work. What is at issue is using this exclusivity as a general veto against consumer protection.

Whenever the platform invokes exclusive ownership, business secrecy, licensing or the proprietary structure of the ecosystem to resist control of the mode of supply, the reconciliation must be made in light of the social function and of the constitutional limits on the exercise of private positions.<1>p. 747</1>

In this scenario, intellectual property appears as an infrastructure of semiotic and technical governance. It not only protects creations, but contributes to delimiting uses, restricting reconfigurations and consolidating the supplier's authority over the conditions of enjoyment<1>p. 130</1>
Licenses and technical restrictions are not treated merely as contractual content<1>p. 54</1>
which delimits what can be used, for how long, under what conditions<1>p. 54</1>
The corresponding duty is to exercise exclusivity without converting it into a shield for absolute opacity, degrading mutability or arbitrary suppression of enjoyment.<1>p. 747</1>

The minimum required proof falls on the relation between the prerogative invoked and the concrete aspect of the conflict, demonstrating whether the restriction is really necessary to protect the asset or whether it in fact operates as undue immunization of governance.<1>p. 747</1>
The possible legal qualification preserves the validity of intellectual property on its own plane, but rules out its invocation as a general veto on the application of the CDC.<1>p. 747</1>

institutional consequence consists in reconciling exclusivity and consumer protection through delimited auditability, control of functional equivalence and subjection of the exercise of IP to the duties of adequacy, transparency and restoration.<1>p. 748</1>
If the platform owns the place, the currency and the clock, who writes the rules that apply in there?

Why give all this a name?
Isis before Ra, the Sun god, in a line that recalls Egyptian painting without copying any existing work. At the Sun's feet, a small serpent made of his own light.

It all began with a simple question, whether the skin is yours. Along the way, a kind of consumption appeared in which you imagine you are standing on your own ground, but you are only walking on borrowed ground, which can be taken away and remade at any moment.

On this ground, access, permanence and even the meaning of what you bought depend on an administration that never stops. And this administration does not present itself as someone's management. It presents itself as technical normality, as the way things are.

The crossing carried out in this work began with the observation that there is a kind of consumption in which the subject imagines being on their own ground, but only moves within a granted, revocable and reconfigurable ground.<1>p. 791</1>
Access, permanence and even the meaning of what was acquired depend on a continuous administration that does not present itself as management, but as technical normality.<1>p. 21</1>
The way out is not to tear everything down. That would be like wanting to put out the sun to get rid of the shadow. It is not about freezing the services or pretending they are simple.
The goal is different, more modest and firmer. It is to tame the inequality without destroying the structure, with clear criteria. It is to contain instead of demolish.

Charting a way forward, however, does not mean seeking a heroic gesture of demolition, as if it were desirable to put out the sun to solve the problem of the shadow. Charting a way forward means proposing criteria capable of taming the asymmetry without destroying the infrastructure.<1>p. 791</1>
It is in this sense that the proposed protection is organized as an ethics of containment, not as an ethics of demolition.<1>p. 793</1>
Not to freeze the service, nor to deny the complexity of the environment<1>p. 755</1>
What does the myth of Isis and Ra teach about naming?

An Egyptian myth helps make this clear. Ra, the Sun god, reigned over all, but he was not invulnerable. Isis did not want to destroy the Sun. She only wanted him to acknowledge that he was not absolute.

With a serpent made of Ra's own substance, she poisoned him. In exchange for the cure, she asked for a single thing, the secret name he kept to himself. And the effect was decisive. Once named, power stops being pure presence, which is simply there, and becomes something that can be called upon, delimited and made to answer for what it does.
Ra reigns over all, but he is not invulnerable.<1>p. 792</1>
At the same time, Isis does not wish to annihilate the sun.<1>p. 792</1>
Her interest is to force the sun to acknowledge that it is not absolute.<1>p. 792</1>
Isis produces the serpent from the substance of Ra himself and, with this, turns the excess of power into an instrument for manifesting its limit.<1>p. 792</1>
In exchange for the cure, Isis demands only that Ra reveal to her the name he keeps to himself.<1>p. 792</1>
Once named, power ceases to operate as pure natural presence and becomes invocable, delimitable and, therefore, obliged to answer for its acts.<1>p. 792</1>

That is what the names along this path do. As long as the platform can say that it merely works, merely updates and merely applies rules, the discussion stays trapped in the language of the inevitable, and nobody sues the rain.

When it is shown that access, permanence, visibility, reputation and use are organized by design and by punishment, what looked like weather looks like a decision again. And what looks like a decision again can be controlled.
As long as the platform can say that it merely works, merely updates, merely executes, merely applies rules, the conflict will remain trapped in the idiom of the inevitable.<1>p. 792</1>
what previously looked like weather looks like a decision again. And what looks like a decision again can be controlled.<1>p. 793</1>

What Brazilian consumer law lacks in the face of the law of the platform is not indignation or the rhetoric of denunciation. It lacks the vocabulary to show and prove decisions that today pass for the mere functioning of the system.

Naming, here, is not writing poetry. It is taking power out of the place of the obvious, where nobody questions it, and bringing it to the place of what can be contested. That is why this path gave a name to each thing you may already have felt without knowing how to say it.

What Consumer Law lacks in the face of the Lex Plataformae is not moral indignation, nor a rhetorical repertoire of denunciation. It lacks the vocabulary to make demonstrable those decisions that today pass for the mere functioning of the system.<1>p. 792</1>
Naming is not poeticizing. Naming is shifting power from a regime of self-evidence to a regime of contestability.<1>p. 792</1>
And what would you ask about your skin now?

Why does all this seem normal?
Clouds hung by wires from scaffolding, like a theater set, and rain falling on people with umbrellas who look down and do not see the wires.

You have probably heard that this is how it works, that it was just an update or that this is the rule of the game. Phrases like these make a choice look like a thing of nature, which nobody decided and which nobody could have decided differently.

And this does not happen only in games, which merely let you see, almost with the naked eye, the production of dependence and of symbolic value. Outside them, in apps for work, study, reputation and shopping, the same effects are usually presented as inevitable, and not as design choices. As long as the platform can say that it merely works, merely updates and merely applies rules, the conflict stays trapped in the language of the inevitable.

If the experience of interactive entertainment allows one to see, almost with the naked eye, the production of dependence, the fabrication of symbolic value, the conversion of routine into bond and the naturalization of asymmetries<1>p. 23</1>

This is where the law comes in. One of its functions is to name what, without a name, becomes bad luck, the rule of the game or technical necessity. When it works, the law prevents the will of the strongest from becoming normality just because they can impose it.

Law is the language of the earthly gods. It is the way in which the collectivity that organizes itself as a State transforms forces into forms, conflicts into criteria, desires into limits and powers into responsibilities. When it works, it prevents the will of the strongest from becoming normality through sheer capacity for imposition. It names and organizes what, without a name, becomes “bad luck”, “the rule of the game” or “technical necessity”.<1>p. 23</1>
Why does nobody sue the rain?
Nobody sues the rain, because weather happens and we make do. That is why, when a loss arrives looking like weather, nobody thinks of complaining, and life goes on.

On a platform, though, this weather is manufactured and comes in a predictable sequence, with a shallow explanation and an appearance of total normality. The harm stops being an event and becomes part of the routine of whoever governs the place. And when a company starts to govern your participation as if it were weather, and not a choice that can be controlled, the law is already too late.

Technique comes to operate as a manifest language, that is, fully operative. A language of architecture and engineering that defines what can be seen, proven, contested, repaired and even remembered. It manufactures facts of consumption the way one manufactures weather in a predictable sequence, with superficial justification and an appearance of strict normality. The harm ceases to be an event, since it is part of the very routine of government.<1>p. 32</1>
Because when private power begins to govern participation as if it were weather, and not an institutionally controllable choice, the Law is already far too late.<1>p. 755</1>
<1>Technique and media</1>Autonomy of technique

Technique usually seems to move on its own. It always chooses the most efficient means, and, once what is efficient has been defined, it grows by itself and spreads. Over time, it starts to impose its logic, as if nobody were deciding anything, and the criterion for decisions simply becomes what works best.
That is why so much change arrives with the excuse of efficiency. It seems the machine asked for it, and not that someone wanted it.

Jacques Ellul <1>(1968)</1> describes technique as a system that ceases to operate as a mere instrument and comes to present itself as a reality of its own, no longer limited to being a means, but capable of imposing its logic as an object in itself<2>p. 86</2>

This dynamic is oriented by efficiency and tends to automatically select the most effective method, so that, once the criterion of efficiency has been measured and established, technique consolidates and expands by its own force<1>p. 86</1>

In this scenario, values and purposes lose centrality because technical rationality operates as a machine of instrumentalization, converting everything into a means and shifting the decision criterion to the performance of the method and to what works best<1>p. 86</1>
<1>Technique and media</1>Media as a form of life

The medium changes what counts. When television took the place of the printed word as the main form of public conversation, appearance and performance gained weight over argument. It was not only the way of saying things that changed, but what seemed important and what seemed true.

The same happens on platforms, only more strongly. It is the screen that decides what appears first, what can be understood and what seems true. Personalizing, ranking and measuring are not mere features of an app, because they carry criteria of value and visibility that guide the behavior of millions of people.

In Amusing Ourselves to Death, the author analyzes how television, by replacing the printed word as the main medium of public communication, reorganizes the form of discourse and, with this, reconfigures cultural content itself<1>p. 89</1>
In the political field, visual logic shifts the weight of argument to appearance, performance and impression management<1>p. 89</1>
Neil Postman shifts the problem to media as a form of life, showing that the means of communication alter criteria of relevance, intelligibility and socially practicable truth.<1>p. 85-86</1>
Personalization, ranking and metrification do not constitute mere functionalities, since they materialize criteria of value and visibility that guide behavior at scale.<1>p. 90</1>
<1>Technique and media</1>Desymbolization

Advertising takes symbols from culture, such as friendship, courage and prestige, and sticks them onto products, as if buying solved needs for affection and for a place in the group. Over time, these symbols wear out, and the capacity to give meaning to one's own experiences becomes poorer and more fragmented.

In the digital world, this does not stay in the ad, because it becomes design, and the screen decides when, how and for whom each sign appears, repeats and is rewarded. Manipulation, then, is not only in the content of the message, but in the way it is distributed.
For the author, companies mobilize cultural symbols to attribute to material products the illusory capacity to satisfy emotional and social needs<1>p. 90</1>

42 According to Willem H. Vanderburg <1>(2016)</1>, cultural desymbolization represents the process of weakening the human capacity to attribute meaning to experiences, resulting in a fragmented and impoverished understanding of life as a whole<2>p. 90</2>
desymbolization does not act only in advertising discourse, but couples itself to technical architectures that administer visibility, repetition and reward<1>p. 91</1>

Semiotic manipulation, therefore, does not occur only through the content of messages, but through the form of their distribution and through the interface logic that defines when, how and for whom certain signs appear.<1>p. 91</1>
<1>Technique and media</1>Technical code

But technique does not fall from the sky, because someone decides what it does. Screens, locks, permissions, rewards and punishments carry social and economic purposes. If technology is made by people, concrete design choices matter to the law.

The code is the set of decisions that defines what a system does. If this code is written by people, it has a direction, and a direction can be reconstructed, examined and criticized. There is no fatalism in this, because what was chosen could also have been chosen differently.
Andrew Feenberg's critique prevents this diagnosis from being received as fatalism.<1>p. 86</1>

If technology is a social construction, concrete mediations matter legally: interfaces, frictions, permissions, incentives and punishments materialize social and economic purposes in artifacts and platforms.<1>p. 86</1>
For this reason, technical architecture is not a mere support of the consumer relationship<1>p. 86</1>
If the technical code is determined by actors, it is politically situated and economically orientable and, therefore, its teleologies can be reconstructed and criticized.<1>p. 135</1>

So the skin that changes, the character remade from scratch and the punishment that keeps escalating all the way to a ban are not natural effects of a technology that evolves. They are design decisions, because someone decided it would be this way, and that decision is something you can ask questions about.

The alteration of a rare cosmetic, the reconfiguration of a character by rework and the gradation of sanctions up to the ban are not natural effects of an evolving technology, but architectural decisions<1>p. 120-121</1>
<1>Semiotics and language</1>Reading codes

To read a sign, you need to know the code. A red light in traffic only means stop because everyone learned the rule. In the game, rarity, level, badge and border color work the same way, and only make sense to those who know the rule that organizes them.

The difference is who writes the rule, which in traffic is the law. Inside the game, whoever defines the codes, the categories and what counts as an important difference is the platform itself. It is the platform that decides what is rare, what is common and what each mark means.

[...] semiotics is treated here as a material dimension of the legal problem, not as an interpretive ornament. [...] In this key, Umberto Eco's contribution allows us to understand how codes and conventions make the performance legible and organize the consumer's expectation<1>p. 261</1>
There is an asymmetry of meaning, linked to control over reading codes, categories and classifications that define what counts as a relevant difference.<1>p. 322</1>
<1>Semiotic vulnerability</1>
Remember the purchase in the shop window and the license in the contract? This friction, simple and easy to check, is the clearest picture of a disadvantage that goes beyond knowing or not knowing.

You can read every line of the terms of use and still be unable to check whether you received what was promised. This is not because you weren't paying attention. The meaning of things in there is fixed by rules and records the platform controls, including what has value, what is rare and what counts as an error. It is the platform that decides which links between things stay visible and which paths of reading stay open to you.

That is why the problem stops being knowing more and becomes being able to find your bearings and react. When the environment controls what appears, what is recognized and how consequences are distributed, it becomes harder to plan, to foresee what will happen and to contest a decision. What you face is an inequality of understanding and of capacity to act, created by the way the platform governs the place.
It is in this friction, simple and verifiable, that semiotic vulnerability becomes intelligible.<1>p. 401</1>

the promise is not auditable through individual reading alone, because the meaning that sustains value and enjoyment is stabilized by rules and records of the ecosystem, while the platform controls which correlations will be activated and which reading paths will be made available<1>p. 281</1>
Semiotic vulnerability describes, on this plane, a structural loss of the capacity for verification, and not a defect of the consumer's attention.<1>p. 281</1>

When the environment controls the parameters of appearance, recognition and commensuration that structure value and belonging, and keeps opaque the criteria for distributing consequences, the possibility of planning conduct, anticipating effects and contesting decisions is structurally weakened. The problem then shifts from "knowing more" to "being able to find one's bearings and react".<1>p. 396</1>

Semiotic vulnerability can be defined, in summary, as the objective condition of the consumer's exposure to a structural inequality of intelligibility and agency in platform-governed ecosystems of enjoyment<1>p. 396</1>
Who keeps the records of what happened?

There is a detail that makes the disadvantage of those who only see the environment from outside even more serious. Whoever controls the way things are shown usually also controls the records that would allow reconstructing what happened. The old versions of the screens, the criteria for highlighting, the history of changes and the traces of each decision stay with the platform.
In other words, the inequality of meaning usually comes together with an inequality of proof. Whoever designed the screen that confused you is the one who keeps the snapshot of what it looked like.

The particularity of this mechanism lies in the fact that the asymmetry of meaning tends to come with an asymmetry of proof. Whoever controls the form by which the object is made intelligible frequently also controls the records by which this intelligibility can be reconstructed in case of conflict.<1>p. 720</1>
Logs, interface histories, screen versions, curation criteria, change records, visibility parameters and decision traces<1>p. 720</1>
<1>Performative transparency</1><2><3>Performative transparency</3></2>

Too much information can also hide things. There are layered documents, links that lead to other links, cross-references, overly technical language, the important detail in fine print and the irrelevant one highlighted, and cascades of warnings. In the end, you receive text, but you do not receive guidance.

It is transparency as theater, in which the platform puts on a show of opening everything up while keeping up a noise that, in practice, has the same effect as hiding. The problem is not missing information, but the excess, the dispersion and the wrong ordering of what is essential.

Successive layers of documents, serialized links, cross-references, excessively technical language, inverted visual emphasis, cascading disclaimers and the displacement of relevant content to improbable zones of the contracting flow can produce the same legal effect as omission.<1>p. 619</1>
The consumer receives text, but does not receive guidance. The platform stages informational openness while maintaining, under an appearance of compliance, a regime of noise.<1>p. 619-620</1>
Performative transparency does not consist in the absence of information, but in the excess, dispersion and defective hierarchization of essential content.<1>p. 620</1>
<1>Meaning-vitiated consent</1><2><3>Meaning-vitiated consent</3></2>

You clicked accept, but you accepted within a frame of language that already left you outside the center of the relationship. It was not a mistake about a price or a deadline, which can be pointed out and corrected.

It was something deeper, because the very way the product was supplied made it hard to decipher, compare and foresee the consequences that mattered. You received the text, but you did not receive the key to understand the code that gives it meaning. It is a controlled incapacity, produced by the conditions of communication, and not carelessness on your part.

The consumer does not merely get one piece of data wrong. They adhere within a frame of language that already places them outside the center of intelligibility of the relationship. It is at this point that one can speak of meaning-vitiated consent. It is not a matter of a one-off factual error, such as confusing a price or an isolated deadline.<1>p. 603</1>
The consumer receives the text, but does not receive real access to the code that organizes its meaning.<1>p. 603</1>
It is a controlled incapacity.<1>p. 603</1>
structurally produced, by the communicational conditions of supply, to decode, compare and anticipate relevant consequences<1>p. 604</1>

Why not just call all this digital vulnerability? Because that expression says where the injury happens, but does not show the machinery. Digital is the setting, and, to arrive at duties, proof and redress, you need to pin down the mechanism that produces the disadvantage, and that is what semiotic vulnerability does.

The expression “digital vulnerability” will not be adopted here because, although descriptively useful, it offers little dogmatic yield. It names the environment in which the injury occurs, but does not isolate the legally relevant mechanism of the asymmetry.<1>p. 584</1>
In this vocabulary, the “digital” works as a marker of setting, not as an operator of imputation.<1>p. 584</1>
stabilizing what matters for duty, proof, unlawfulness and remedy<1>p. 584-585</1>
Does every digital environment put you at a disadvantage?

This does not mean that every digital environment makes you vulnerable in this sense, nor that you are incapable in the face of technology. The disadvantage that counts is not a generic attribute of the digital nor a failing of yours. It is the one that arises when the signs, screens and records that guide your decision are controlled by whoever is on the other side.

The vulnerability relevant to the application of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption cannot be understood as a generic attribute of the digital, nor be reduced to economic hyposufficiency or to the consumer's lesser individual aptitude to understand technically complex environments.<1>p. 719</1>
Nor is it a matter of presupposing absolute incapacity in the face of the digital.<1>p. 720</1>
<1>The platform cannot design the experience to keep you from understanding</1><2>The platform cannot design the experience to keep you from understanding</2>
When do the signs on the screen weigh against you?

Almost everything you know about your skin passes through screens, notices, icons and paths that the platform designs. It is through them that you find out how much it is worth, what risk you run when buying and how to complain if something goes wrong. When your expectation and your chance to contest depend on these signs controlled by the company, you are in a fragile position. And the law takes this fragility into account.

This fragility has nothing to do with naivety, lack of attention or little familiarity with technology. It arises from the way the environment is set up. Whoever designs the screen decides what is highlighted, what is hidden and in what order things appear. And they usually also keep the records that would allow the story to be told later.
How should the platform set up the experience?

By not setting up the experience in a way that only the platform understands. The design of the environment needs to respect good faith, which is the duty of loyalty between the parties, as well as transparency and a real chance for you to understand what you are using.
How do you show the path that led to your decision?

Through the path you took inside the game up to the purchase or the problem, what was highlighted on the screen and where the information appeared. The records that make it possible to reconstruct how your expectation was formed also matter. Dated screenshots, screen recordings and the purchase and confirmation screens help, because they show how the environment was set up, and not only what you remember.
What can you ask for when the environment is to blame?

That the problem be treated as a matter of the environment, and not as carelessness on your part. If this dependence on the platform's signs is demonstrated, stronger duties to inform, advertise clearly and present proof may apply. Depending on the case, the practice may be seen as abusive, as insufficient information or as deception by ambiguity or by omission. Added to other elements, this may even change who needs to prove what.
Does every complicated game violate rights?

This does not mean that every complicated game violates rights, nor that you are incapable in the face of the digital. The fragility that counts is the one that appears when the signs controlled by the platform steer your expectation or hinder your reaction.

Whenever expectation, perception of value, risk assessment or capacity to contest depend on signs, interfaces, flows and informational trails controlled by the supplier, there will be legally relevant semiotic vulnerability.<1>p. 744</1>
The term does not designate naivety, credulity or cultural deficiency of the consumer.<1>p. 719</1>
Whoever controls the form by which the object is made intelligible often also controls the records by which this intelligibility can be reconstructed in the event of a conflict.<1>p. 720</1>
The corresponding duty is not to organize the experience through a structural asymmetry of meaning incompatible with good faith, transparency and legibility of enjoyment.<1>p. 744</1>

The minimum required proof involves reconstructing the user's journey, the informational architecture of the environment, the communicational salience, the paths of understanding and the records available to reconstitute the formation of the expectation.<1>p. 744</1>
The first source of support is interface trails and decision flow: dated screenshots, screen recordings, purchase, acceptance, upgrade and confirmation screens<1>p. 607</1>
What is relevant there is not the user's subjective memory<1>p. 607</1>

The possible legal qualification may support abusive practice, informational insufficiency, deceptiveness by ambiguity or relevant omission and, when articulated with other elements, grounds for dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof.<1>p. 744</1>

The institutional consequence consists in bringing the conflict back to the governance of the environment, avoiding moralization of the consumer's conduct and allowing reinforced duties of information, advertising and proof to apply.<1>p. 744</1>

The artificial intelligence assistant changed or got it wrong. What can I demand? · Lex Plataformae
<1>Problems</1>
<1>Your rights</1> · <2>By problem</2>
<1>The artificial intelligence assistant changed or got it wrong.</1> <2>What can I demand?</2>

You used an artificial intelligence assistant, the kind of program that chats, summarizes and gives guidance, and the answer turned out to be wrong or the service started working differently. The problem goes beyond the wrong sentence, because the value of this service lies in the trust it asks of you and in your chance to reconstruct what happened.
What is at stake is not only the content issued, but the regime of functional trust in which this content is received, used and converted into conduct.<1>p. 758</1>
When does the assistant's error stop being just a bad answer?

What matters is the way the answer reached you. There may be a problem when it seems more certain and complete than the service really is. There may also be one when you cannot understand why you got that answer or whether the assistant changed.

Version changes count too, meaning the moments when the company swaps the program running behind the assistant. They can alter results and cut features without canceling your access, so the fact that the assistant still opens does not prove that nothing changed.
The service does not need to have lied for the problem to count. It may be enough that it trades clarity for an appearance of trust and leaves you with the cost of the error, the review or the loss.

There may be informational noise when the architecture of the answer projects an appearance of safety, completeness or sufficiency incompatible with the real limits of the service. There may be functional opacity when the user cannot reconstruct, in minimally verifiable terms, why a given output was presented to them, to what extent there was a relevant change in the system's behavior or which elements of the environment conditioned the answer that guided their conduct.<1>p. 759</1>

Modulation is constitutive, given that version changes, parameter adjustments, policy revisions, performance variations and reconfigurations of safeguards can alter results, restrict functionalities or reorganize costs of enjoyment without formal cancellation of access.<1>p. 487</1>

There may also be acute evidentiary asymmetry when the functional impact of the service depends on history, interactional context, internal parameters or records that remain concentrated with the supplier. In these scenarios, the injury does not need to appear as a direct lie to be legally relevant. It is enough that the environment replaces legibility with a performance of trust, shifting to the user the cost of bearing error, review, oscillation or functional loss without adequate institutional trails of reconstruction.<1>p. 759</1>
Which parts of the conversation with the assistant are worth saving?

Save the whole conversation, and not only the wrong answer, including what you asked, the warnings that appeared or were missing and the way the answer was shown. It helps to record what you did based on it, because the weight it carried in your decision is part of the case. A generic warning that the system may make mistakes does not settle the matter on its own, and the answer should not be judged apart from what made it seem reliable.
Part of the history and records stays only with the company. That is why your protection should not depend only on what you managed to save, since the rest was never in your hands.

The relevant evidence tends to require reconstruction of the informational journey, the context of use, the available interactional history, the warnings present or absent, the way the answer was presented and the practical function it served in the user's decision. It also tends to require caution regarding recurring blind spots. The first is the tendency to reduce the conflict to the sentence issued, ignoring the semiotic architecture that made it reliable or operational. The second is the tendency to presume that generic warnings about the system's limitations would suffice, by themselves, to neutralize any problem of informational adequacy.<1>p. 759-760</1>
What can you ask for besides a correct answer?

Depending on the case, the request may include access to the conversation history and its minimum records. It may also include a sufficient explanation of the limits that matter and clarity about changes in how the service can be used. The goal is to make it possible to link what was promised to the effect you suffered.

The failure may be treated as a problem with the quality of the information the service delivers or as a breach of the duty to inform. It may also be read as an abusive practice, which is conduct that Brazilian consumer law prohibits, when it stems from a lack of transparency about how the service works. The most fitting response tends to be correcting how it works and communicates and restoring trust, rather than simply paying compensation.

It is a matter of recognizing that, in services whose usefulness lies in cognitively guiding the user, there must be minimum institutional verifiability over relevant aspects of the service. This includes, depending on the case, preservation of accessible history, minimum interaction traces, sufficient disclosure of materially relevant limits, intelligibility about changes in the regime of use and the possibility of reconstructing the link between the service's functional promise and the impact produced on the user's experience.<1>p. 759</1>
Where can you take a problem with the assistant?

The first path is usually the company itself, with a request for the history and an explanation of what changed. Since the decisive records tend to stay with it, a lawyer helps when the case depends on asking for those records to be kept and shown.

If the same lack of clarity affects everyone who uses the service, because it is part of the normal way it works, the response can be collective. Procon (the state consumer protection agency), Consumidor.gov.br (the federal government's online complaint platform), the Public Prosecutor's Office and the Public Defender's Office are paths that the channels page details.

Whoever controls the service controls, to a large extent, the decisive records of the relationship. Logs, version histories, transactions, interface parameters, change notices and relevant technical documentation tend to remain in the supplier's possession. For this reason, operationalizing the category must go hand in hand with requests for the preservation and disclosure of minimum documentation of the supply.<1>p. 608</1>
<1>The complaint channels and the deadlines</1>
How far can your demands on an assistant go?

The protection does not go as far as requiring the company to open up the model, the code or the inner workings of the assistant. What you can ask for is the minimum needed to check what matters in your case.

Not every digital service that changes over time falls under the same protection, and an artificial intelligence label alone does not bring it in. The strongest reading is that the very design of the service exploits those who use it. That reading may fit the most serious cases, when the lack of transparency is a stable part of the way the service is exploited.

My account was blocked or banned. What about what I bought? · Lex Plataformae
<1>My account was blocked or banned.</1> <2>What about what I bought?</2>

When your account is blocked or banned, which means permanent expulsion, you also lose access to everything in it, including what you bought. The company can punish, but the punishment needs a reason that can be checked and a real way for you to defend yourself.

If the account is terminated, access is lost not only to the “game”, but to the set of data and virtual content that structured the experience, in addition to the assertion that there is no refund in cases of just cause<1>p. 375</1>

In platform ecosystems, sanctions do not operate merely as a one-off disciplinary response to conduct attributed to the user. They can affect access, permanence, visibility, reputation, relational insertion and continuity of enjoyment. For this reason, they must be controlled by denser criteria than the mere formal existence of sanctioning power. They require verifiable reasoning, decisional coherence and intelligible avenues of contestation.<1>p. 749</1>
How do you know whether the punishment went too far?

Punishment is not always expulsion. Often the account stays active but becomes less visible, loses rewards and has its chat cut off, and this also takes value from what you bought, because staying in on worse terms is already a loss.

The warning sign appears when the punishment comes without a reason you can understand or when the path to contest it leads nowhere. It also appears when undoing the measure is much harder than applying it was.

Many punishments come from automatic detection. In League of Legends, for example, the company itself warns that the punishment may arrive up to 15 minutes after the end of the match. These punishments follow criteria the company does not fully reveal, and it is this lack of clarity that makes the punishment so hard to contest.
The second form is ex post enforcement, in which the ecosystem applies declared or partially declared sanctions after a moderation event or automatic detection.<1>p. 373</1>

In the Instant Feedback System, Riot states that users may be punished “up to 15 minutes after the end of the match”, and describes a range of consequences running from restrictions to permanent suspensions<1>p. 375</1>

The legal consequence is that the sanction becomes part of the object itself, since it defines the practical stability of the acquired position and conditions continued access on criteria whose detailed functioning is not fully revealed to the user, under justifications of efficiency, prevention of cheating and management of scale<1>p. 375</1>
Which records are worth gathering right after the punishment?

Keep the punishment notice with its date, the message explaining the reason, if there is one, and every reply you got when you contested it. Screenshots of the inventory, the history and the purchases while you can still see them also help, as do the emails and receipts for the purchases, because after the block they are what lets you reconstruct what you had.

The rest usually stays with the company, which keeps the type of punishment applied, the reason and the effect it had on the account. That is why your request can ask it to preserve and show these records.

What is required here is not a total sweep of the system, but a minimum documentary core: history of relevant versions; essential change records with functional impact; trails of consent and decision flow; history of relevant transactions; communications of change; and, when there is enforcement, basic records of the decision event, such as the category applied, reason and consequence.<1>p. 658</1>

Given the concentration of records, preservation and disclosure of supply trails are warranted, with rational redistribution of the burden and presumptions favorable to the consumer when the supplier does not cooperate or keeps the proof in a black box.<1>p. 609</1>
What can you ask for when the account was closed without explanation?

If the punishment has neither a reason that can be checked nor a reasonable way to contest it, you can ask for it to be reviewed or undone. You can also ask the company to say which punishment it applied and why, and to offer a way to contest it that actually works.

The first thing to seek is getting back what was taken, such as access, history and inventory, when that is possible. In more serious cases, losing the account, the history or years of your journey may even be treated as moral damages, which is harm to the person and not only to the wallet. But a mere annoyance is not enough for that.
Brazil's data protection law (the LGPD) also helps, because the block does not take away your right to ask the company to confirm that it holds data about you and to give you access to it.

The use of data linked to the consumer's trajectory, history and digital biography must remain compatible with the purposes disclosed and with the context of the relationship, needs to be intelligible to the data subject, and does not eliminate the rights to confirmation of existence, access, correction, deletion or portability of processed data.<1>p. 542</1>
Where can you turn when support only repeats that the decision is final?
The first path is the company's own channel for contesting decisions, because it must offer one that really works. There you can ask for the concrete reason and the records of the punishment.

If the company neither explains nor reviews the punishment, the case can go on through Procon, Consumidor.gov.br or the Small Claims Court (Juizado Especial Cível), paths that the channels page details. In a lawsuit, the judge can order the company to show the records and split the burden of proof according to who has access to them.

When many people are punished the same way, the response can go beyond your case and reach the punishment system itself, through a collective action or through the action of public consumer protection bodies.

When the litigation reveals a repeated pattern of opacity, abusive reconfiguration or non-verifiable suppression of functional value, the response need not be limited to the individual case.<1>p. 662</1>

Without opening a parallel regulatory front, the subsection shows that open auditability and functional equivalence can also guide the action of protection bodies in platform markets. These standards offer a concrete criterion for consent decrees, recommendations, civil investigations and minimum governance requirements: functional impact reports on relevant changes, verifiable transparency protocols, preservation of essential records, understandable contestation procedures and minimum criteria of restoration in case of relevant degradation of enjoyment.<1>p. 662-663</1>
How far does the defense of someone who was punished go?

The company has the power to punish, and having that power is not the problem. What is required is that the punishment have a reason that can be checked, consistency from one decision to the next and an understandable way to contest it.

The terms of use, which are the contract you accept when creating the account, usually say there is no refund when the account is terminated for just cause, which is a serious reason attributed to you. This clause carries weight, but it does not turn the erasure of the whole account into a simple internal adjustment, immune to any control.

None of this guarantees that the account comes back, because each case depends on what happened and on what can be shown. And the data protection law does not make you the owner of everything the company records about your account.

Clause 2.3 of Riot's Terms of Service provides that, once the account is terminated, the user loses access to the account, the associated data, the game currency and the virtual content, without refund in cases of just cause, with the further possibility of cancellation of other accounts and of access to other services<1>p. 540</1>

Exclusivity is exercised, here, as a power of complete erasure of the consumed experience, which prevents treating sanction, exclusion or rollback as mere internal adjustments without existential legal relevance.<1>p. 541</1>

The use of data linked to the consumer's trajectory, history and digital biography must remain compatible with the purposes disclosed and with the context of the relationship, needs to be intelligible to the data subject, and does not eliminate the rights to confirmation of existence, access, correction, deletion or portability of processed data. It also presupposes secure management of relevant records and trails. These provisions do not turn the consumer into the absolute owner of everything the platform records<1>p. 542</1>

My child spent money in a game. What does the law say? · Lex Plataformae
<1>My child spent money in a game.</1> <2>What does the law say?</2>

Your child spent money in a game, on small repeated purchases, on loot boxes or on offers that came back with every event. Brazilian law already sees children and adolescents as an audience that calls for special care in these environments, and there are specific rules on what can be offered to them.
The focus on minors thus works as an institutional trigger to make visible asymmetries of understanding and of capacity to contest in environments governed by architecture.<1>p. 494</1>

The norm goes beyond mere programmatic discourse by banning loot boxes in games aimed at children and adolescents and by prohibiting profiling techniques for targeting commercial advertising.<1>p. 545</1>
How does the game weigh on a child's or an adolescent's purchases?

In games that keep being updated and keep selling things after you install them, the purchase is rarely a one-off. It comes in pieces, pulled along by return cycles, urgency notices, promises of progress, comparison with friends and incentives built into the game itself.

That is why the law also looks at how the game works, and not only at what appears on the screen. The age rating, which tells you what age the game is suitable for, takes into account the risks of microtransactions, the small purchases made inside the game.

When promises of progress, the wish to belong to the group and advertising inside the game add up, the effects can reach beyond the child. They can reach the family, which then has to pay closer attention and may see its income affected.

In games operated as a service, consumption decisions tend to be fragmented over time, mediated by return cycles, urgency signals, promises of progression, social comparison and incentives embedded in the very design of enjoyment.<1>p. 494</1>
In a significant share of cases, the risk lies in the way the environment of enjoyment itself works.<1>p. 494</1>
Paragraph 2. In carrying out the indicative age rating of electronic games, the risks related to the use of microtransaction mechanisms shall be taken into account.<1>p. 544</1>

The effects radiate onto the family, generating expenses with treatment, demanding greater attention from guardians and interfering with family income <1>Torres</1><2>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 23-24)</2>.<3>p. 673</3>
Which records help show how the spending happened?

It is worth keeping the statements and emails for each purchase, the store and confirmation screens, and the event, deadline or offer notices that appeared in the game. These records show how the environment was set up, and that counts for more than your memory of each purchase.
It also helps to note the game's age rating and whether it is made for children and adolescents or is likely to be used by them. This changes the rules that apply to loot boxes.
What can the family demand from whoever supplies the game?

Anyone who offers digital products and services to children and adolescents has duties to prevent risks, to protect, to inform and to provide security, always guided by their best interest. That best interest includes privacy, security, mental and physical health, access to information and well-being.

In games aimed at this audience, or that it is likely to access, the law prohibits loot boxes. It also prohibits techniques that build a profile of the child to target advertising at them. If the spending was on a box like that, the complaint can point to this prohibition.

In addition, the general consumer rules apply, because having a specific law for games does not set aside consumer law. The games law itself places consumer protection and the full protection of children and adolescents among its principles.

The Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents reinforces this diagnosis by making explicit, on another normative front, that the digital environment is not neutral and that suppliers are subject to positive duties of prevention, protection, information and security. The very material content of the best interest of children and adolescents, in this context, already encompasses privacy, security, mental and physical health, access to information, freedom to participate in society and well-being.<1>p. 545</1>
Where can the family turn?

The first place to go is the company itself. Anyone who supplies these services in Brazil must keep a legal representative here with powers to receive service of process, which is the formal notice that there is a lawsuit.

A public authority, the National Data Protection Agency (ANPD), is also in charge of enforcing these rules. The case can also go through Procon, Consumidor.gov.br or the Small Claims Court, paths detailed on the channels page.

Since the game's design is the same for all the children who play, a problem in it tends to be collective. In that case, the response can come through a collective action or through public consumer protection bodies.

The statute imposes concrete duties to remove content that violates rights and requires a legal representative in the country with powers to receive service of process, while the regulating decree designates an administrative authority, provides for blocking orders and even activates the technical infrastructural layer of the digital environment through coordination with Anatel and CGI.br.<1>p. 547</1>
“Article 1. This Decree [...] designates the National Data Protection Agency - ANPD as an autonomous administrative authority [...].<1>p. 547</1>
This is especially important on platforms, where unlawfulness usually comes in batches, not in a single piece.<1>p. 662</1>
Without opening a parallel regulatory front, the subsection shows that open auditability and functional equivalence can also guide the action of protection bodies in platform markets.<1>p. 662</1>
How far do the rules for children in games go?

The ban on loot boxes is limited in scope. It applies to games aimed at children and adolescents or that they are likely to access, and not to every game. The age rating offers guidance on the suitable age, but it is not a prior authorization from the government.

In view of these rules, one company decided that players under 18 may not play its adult-rated titles in Brazil, even with their guardians' permission. The account could be frozen, with items and progress kept until it was unlocked, so the record stayed but the use stopped.
The games law and the statute help you see the problem, but on their own they do not settle disputes over the use of what was bought.

In this framework, the public policy of indicative age rating plays a useful contextual role. Without working as a prior authorization, it acts as a guiding instrument aimed at informing age suitability and relevant descriptors<1>p. 494</1>

In the text “Age verification”, the company states that, in Brazil, minors under 18 cannot access games rated 18+, even with the guardians' consent, and indicates two possible ways for access to be reopened: the user reaching the age of majority or a possible return of the game to a lower age rating <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, [2026]n)</2>.<3>p. 546</3>

I paid a lot for something exclusive, and it came back cheaper. Is that allowed? · Lex Plataformae
<1>I paid a lot for something exclusive, and it came back cheaper.</1> <2>Is that allowed?</2>

You paid more because the item was rare, a special edition or a last chance, and later it went back on sale for less, in another store or in another currency. When exclusivity was used to justify the price, it becomes part of what was sold, and undoing it later can have consequences.

When the platform sells an item at a high price under the promise of exclusivity, or presents exclusivity as a relevant attribute to justify price and spending, it incorporates this quality into the content of the offer and into the perceived utility of the object.<1>p. 213</1>
How do you know whether rarity was part of what you paid for?

A digital item can be copied at almost no cost and sold to everyone, forever. When it becomes rare, disappears from the store or turns into a last chance, that is not down to its nature but to a choice the company made.

This is your case when exclusivity was presented as the reason for the price and the item later came back for much less. It may have come back in an alternative store, in a special currency or in a steep promotion. What defines the problem is that nobody told you clearly, at the time of purchase, that the exclusivity had a time limit.

This is not just vanity. In an item that others see, status, rarity and recognition are part of what you acquired. And the investment also includes the time and the missions you completed to get to it.

For this reason, when a persistent regime of unavailability, exclusivity and last chance is observed in these markets, one is dealing not with a natural condition of the object, but with a deliberate institutional choice, so that scarcity appears not as a fact, but as a project.<1>p. 209</1>

The conflict appears when the platform retroactively reprograms the regime of circulation of the good and allows items previously treated as rare to return to the market in a new acquisition system. In this scenario, the injury perceived by the original holders does not derive from subjective preference, but from the alteration of the foundation that sustained part of the qualitative expectation of consumption, which was the public signal of exclusivity as a position.<1>p. 452-453</1>

In immaterial goods, especially when their enjoyment is publicly visible, utility is inseparable from status, rarity and social recognition, which function as part of the acquired enjoyment bundle.<1>p. 452</1>

In the initial cycle, the specialized press described the means of obtaining it as conditioned on a long list of missions and on the circuit of events, which consolidated rarity as an internal marker of distinction relevant to the ecosystem, and not as a simple ordinary aesthetic variation <1>Marshall</1><2>(Marshall, 2018)</2>. The point in question is important because the “investment”, in this sense, is not translated only into pecuniary value, but also includes time, participation in events and conformity with a specific path.<3>p. 452</3>
What proof of the promise of exclusivity is worth keeping?

It is worth keeping the offer as it appeared, with the words exclusive, rare or last chance, the announced deadline, the price and the currency used. Afterward, it helps to record when and how the item came back, in which store, at what price and in which currency.
What can you ask for when the rarity has been undone?

Depending on the case, the request may include a refund of what was paid, a price reduction or compensation with something that serves the same function. If the item's return caused you further harm that you can demonstrate, there may also be compensation for losses and damages.

The compensation can target the very point of the loss. In a major game, when old rare skins came back to the store, the company announced that the original owners would receive exclusive versions, which could not be bought with the new currency, in recognition of their investment.
You can also ask for the offer to be corrected and honored and for communication that does not match reality to stop.

In a note to the public, the developer states that, when old Prestige skins returned to the store, the original owners would receive exclusive modified versions “in recognition of the investment”, and that these modified versions will not be available for purchase through the new currency then introduced into the ecosystem, Mythic Essence <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2022j)</2>. This is a symbolic restoration aimed directly at the point of loss, preserving a public differential of distinction for the original holders.<3>p. 453</3>
Where can you take a complaint about exclusivity that was undone?

The first step is usually the company itself, with the original offer in hand. The way the item was advertised may be treated as misleading advertising by omission, which is advertising that keeps quiet about what mattered for your decision. The case can also go to Procon and Consumidor.gov.br, both presented on the channels page.
When the same practice is repeated with several items and affects many people, the response can go beyond your case, through the Public Prosecutor's Office or the Public Defender's Office.
When is the item's return not a problem?

Creating scarcity, by itself, is not illegal. Selling in a short window can be legitimate when it does not downgrade what was already bought and when it tells you clearly, at the time, about the duration, the way to get the item, the limits of the offer and the chance of it coming back.
Nor do the buyer's feelings settle the matter on their own. Symbolic value counts when it was part, in a way other people can recognize, of the core of what was sold.
