I lost years of history. Is that more than an item? · Lex Plataformae
<1>I lost years of history.</1> <2>Is that more than an item?</2>

A ban (permanent expulsion from the account), a progress reset or an erasure took away years of history, inventory, achievements and reputation. This loss can go beyond the price of what you bought, because it also takes away the continuity of your own story in that environment.

Clause 2.3 of Riot's Terms of Service provides that, once the account is terminated, the user loses access to the account, the associated data, the game currency and the virtual content, without refund in cases of just cause, with the further possibility of cancellation of other accounts and of access to other services. The clause is valuable because it lays the problem bare: what is lost is not merely an isolated item, but the global position of enjoyment, the history, the inventory, the trajectory and the practical continuity of insertion in the ecosystem<1>p. 540-541</1>
What is lost, in these cases, is not only access, but biographical continuity objectified within the governed regime itself.<1>p. 543</1>
How do you know whether the loss went beyond an item?

What stays in the account over the years is not only access, but history, memory, recognition and the place you occupy there. You built all this with choices, performance, time and purchases, even if within the company's rules, and that is why erasing it is not a simple technical variation.

The loss is usually relevant when you are left out or very limited in participating, or when the conditions of use get substantially worse. It is also relevant when badges, rarities and histories are erased or devalued, or when you stay inside but lose for good the position that gave value to what you had.

The consumer's trajectory is not a mere passive “record” kept by the platform, nor an informational deposit without a subject. It is a biographical result produced by repeated choices, performance, investment of time, acquisition, cooperation, accumulation of signs of belonging and permanence in the ecosystem. Even though this construction occurs under the mediation of the Lex Plataformae, it remains attributable to the consumer as an expression of biographical continuity within the regime of supply.<1>p. 537</1>
What accumulates is a bundle of memory, identity and recognition, so that its unilateral suppression or reclassification cannot be treated as a simple irrelevant technical variation.<1>p. 537</1>
Which records help reconstruct the history that disappeared?

After the erasure, all that is left as proof is old statements, emails, screenshots and your memory. That is why it is worth saving, while you still can, dated screenshots of your profile, inventory, achievements and history.

Even after the loss, you can ask the company to confirm what data it keeps about you and to give you access to it, which helps reconstruct what existed. The company must also store the records that matter securely.
What can you ask for when your whole history has been erased?

The first remedy to seek is restoring what was erased, where that is possible, rather than converting everything straight into money. Brazilian consumer law allows you to demand performance of the obligation or something equivalent, and the judge can seek a practical result that corresponds to that performance.

An erasure, a progress reset or a punishment that wipes out your history needs a reason that can be checked and at least minimal preservation of the records. Where appropriate, you can ask for the position you had to be restored.

In serious cases, losing the account, the history or years of your journey may be treated as moral damages, which is harm to the person, and not only to the wallet. This happens when the loss demonstrably affects your history, your belonging or the reputation and memory built there, and a mere annoyance is not enough.

When the consumer relationship frustrates legitimate expectations as to the adequacy, utility, safety or quality of the service, the consumer protection system is not automatically oriented toward the residual monetization of the loss. It seeks, first of all, to materially restore the consumer's position, satisfy their interests and avoid greater harm, including in a non-patrimonial dimension <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1383; p. 856)</2>. Hence the importance of Article 35 of the CDC<3><4>1</4></3>, which allows one to demand specific performance of the obligation, accept equivalent performance or rescind the contract with losses and damages, and of Article 84 [...] which enshrines specific relief for the obligation and a practical result equivalent to performance.<5>p. 539-540</5>
Who can you ask to give your history back?

The first place to go is the company itself, which runs the account and the records, to ask for the reason for the measure, its records and restoration. It cannot treat your digital history as a black box, a closed system that nobody outside can see into.

If the company does not answer, the case can go on through Procon, Consumidor.gov.br or the Small Claims Court, paths detailed on the channels page. In a lawsuit, the judge can order the company to show the records and split the burden of proof according to who has access to them.
When the erasure or the reset affects many people at once, the response can go beyond your case, through a collective action or through the work of public consumer protection bodies.

The institutional consequence of this reading falls on the platform's governance itself. If it administers access, permanence, visibility, sanctions and trails of participation, then it also administers inclusion and exclusion in the digital social space. Hence the need for minimum parameters of private due process: verifiable reasoning, decisional coherence, procedural predictability and intelligible avenues of contestation. This requirement does not derive from the company's benevolence, but from the public relevance of the effects produced by its governance on the consumer's memory, reputation, continuity of trajectory and symbolic position. The administration of someone else's digital biography cannot operate as a sovereign black box.<1>p. 541-542</1>

The third mechanism is properly procedural: preservation of evidence, disclosure of documents and dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof. When the proof originates and remains under the platform's control, the procedural system cannot feign neutrality.<1>p. 659</1>
How far does the protection of your history on the platform go?

The protection does not make you the owner of everything the company records, nor the author of what you built there. What it requires is that the memory of what you experienced in that environment remain controllable, understandable and minimally accessible.
Ordinary frustrations and normal changes to the service are left out. The loss needs to be significant and persistent, and it must be possible to describe it by criteria that can be checked.
Restoration applies when it is possible and due. When it is not, money remains an option, but as a response that complements or replaces restoration, and not as an automatic reflex to the loss.

It also presupposes secure management of relevant records and trails. These provisions do not turn the consumer into the absolute owner of everything the platform records, but they reinforce that their digital biography is not raw mass entirely unavailable to the data subject and that the administration of the memory of enjoyment must remain controllable, intelligible and minimally accessible.<1>p. 542</1>
Personal integrity, in the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption, does not designate an emotional state or subjective discomfort arising from ordinary market frustrations.<1>p. 457</1>

For this reason, the categories only operate when the downgrading is significant and persistent, when it substantially alters the level of agency and the consumer's position in the ecosystem, and when it can be described by verifiable criteria of loss in the IOC regime, under the filters of relevance and controllability.<1>p. 467-468</1>

What I bought changed in an update. What now? · Lex Plataformae
<1>What I bought changed in an update.</1> <2>What now?</2>

An update, which is the change the company makes to the program after the sale, altered what you bought. The item is still there, but it no longer serves the same way, and what matters is knowing whether the change took away the role that justified the purchase.

Mutability, by itself, is not unlawful. The problem begins when it ceases to operate as a legitimate form of maintenance, improvement or adaptation of supply and starts to degrade, empty or divert, in a relevant way, the function that justified the acquisition and structured the legitimate expectation of enjoyment.<1>p. 729</1>
How do you know whether the update went beyond a simple adjustment?

The typical case is the item that stays in the inventory, with the same name, but has become too weak. It may also have lost an important function or the place it had among the other players. The same goes for a screen redesigned in a way that gets in the way of everyday use, and for a new rule that downgrades what had been promised as equivalent.

The question is not whether the item still exists, nor whether the contract let the company make changes. The question is whether it still fulfills, in essence, the role it had in your experience. This role includes usefulness, the relationship with others and, when it matters, what the item means.
Which proof of the before and after is worth keeping?

It is worth keeping the item's advertisement, with the advantages it promised, because the offer is the yardstick for what had to keep existing. Dated screenshots, recordings and the purchase screens also help, because they show what the item was really like and not only what you remember of it.

Patch notes are the texts in which the company tells what changed in each version. They serve as general information, but rarely let you compare an item before and after. That is why your protection cannot depend on you having archived everything, since the complete version history stays with the company.

The offer and the trust it aroused provide a direct basis for this identification, since the consumer contracts in view of the advantages and qualities advertised, from which arises the legal duty to maintain the conditions offered or, at least, to substantially preserve their utility <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 424)</2>.<3>p. 652</3>
What can you ask for before talking about money?

The first remedy is getting the function back. The request may include undoing the change, when this is technically feasible, or replacing the item with another that serves the same role. It may also include correcting the way the update was carried out.

When the change downgraded what you used in a relevant way, the solution should give you at least a choice. It can be a refund, credit or an exchange for an item of equivalent value. The terms of use, which are the contract you accept when creating the account, help here. Those of a major game already provide for a refund or exchange when a recently bought item is removed entirely.
You can also ask the company to say what changed, when, for what reason and with what effect on the item. And monetary compensation remains possible when restoring is not feasible or not enough.
Where do you start complaining about an update?

The first step is usually the company itself. Continuing to use the service after the change does not mean, by itself, that you agreed to it. Those who have already invested in the account often carry on because they have no way out.

If the company does not answer, a lawyer or the Small Claims Court can help you ask for specific things, such as the version history of that item. They can also ask for an expert examination, carried out by a specialist and limited to what changed. When the same update affected many people, the case can also go to Procon, the Public Defender's Office or the Public Prosecutor's Office, all described on the channels page.
Which changes fall outside this protection?

The company can update, and nobody demands that the item stay identical forever or that the service stand still in time. Small touch-ups, minor changes and normal fluctuations in the life of the service are not enough.

A change only in appearance, as a rule, is left out, and liking the old version better is not enough. It starts to count when the item's symbolic value was the core of what was sold, or when it adds to other signs of a pattern that exploits users.

Even with a relevant loss, the change may still be accepted when the company gives a reason that can be checked. To do so, it must also offer a matching restoration, which means giving back what was lost or something that serves the same function.

The service is going to end. What happens to what I bought? · Lex Plataformae
<1>The service is going to end.</1> <2>What happens to what I bought?</2>

The company announced that it will shut down the game, the app or the service, or turn off the servers, which are the computers on which everything runs. It can end the business, but this right does not include erasing everything without any care for the people who were inside.
How do you know whether the end of the service affects what you had?
What you bought only works while someone keeps the servers on and the environment running. When the service stops, the item may stay in the account, but it stops being good for anything.

The end affects more than loose items. Photos, histories, libraries, contacts, progress, reputation and years of investment go with it, and they do not become worthless just because they are stored in another company's structure.
The contract may call everything a precarious license, which is a permission that can end at any time. Even so, this does not on its own authorize everything to be sacrificed at once.

Photographs, histories, libraries, contact networks, progressions, projected identities, reputational positions and long-term investments cannot be legally treated as residues without density merely because they are technically housed in someone else's infrastructure.<1>p. 796</1>

As relevant portions of contemporary life migrate to private digital ecosystems, the formal precariousness of use licenses can no longer be read as automatic authorization for the complete sacrifice of immaterial objects of consumption incorporated into the consumer's trajectory.<1>p. 709</1>
What is worth saving before the servers are shut down?

It is worth keeping the shutdown announcement, the receipts for what you bought and dated screenshots of your account, library and progress. If it is a program, the invoice, the license and the packaging also matter, because Brazilian law requires them to state how long the version sold will keep working.
The history of your purchases and the company's communications also stay with it, and you can ask for them to be preserved.
What can you ask for when the end is inevitable?

As far as is technically and legally possible, the request may include keeping the service running in another way or letting you take what you have elsewhere. It may also include restoring what was lost or handing the operation over to another company. In short, the exit needs to come with transition, preservation or transfer.
If it is a computer program, whoever sells it must guarantee the technical services that keep it working during the stated period, even after they stop selling it.
And when none of this is possible or enough, monetary compensation remains on the table.
